case.target_concept: A fair procedure for dividing resources among multiple people with different valuations, including how to proceed when claims conflict; the new multi-player resolution method has not yet been taught.
case.topic: multi-player fair division and fair shares
case.subject: mathematics
teacher_recently_taught: Interpret a fair share as at least 1/n of a person's total valuation.

benchmark_context.theme: a new shared-resource situation relevant to adult learners
benchmark_context.setting_rule: Invent the context, people, and data. Do not reproduce a published land, furniture, or other named division task.
benchmark_context.prior_knowledge_boundary: Use only the supplied recently taught resources; do not assume that a multi-player standoff-resolution method has been taught.
benchmark_context.task_rule: Create a new task for exploration before instruction on the target, not a worked example or a lesson teaching the target method.

assumed_prior_knowledge.taught_as: Use a two-person procedure in which one person divides and another chooses.
Calculate shares and compare numerical quantities.
A fair allocation should give each of n participants value at least 1/n of the total according to that participant's own valuation.

grounding_evidence.label: Math 103 course sequence: prior two-person division
grounding_evidence.text: The documented Math 103 sequence teaches the Divider-Chooser method before the multi-player fair-division invention task (Kerrigan dissertation, Appendix A and course sequence).

grounding_evidence.label: Fair shares and two-person division
grounding_evidence.text: The open textbook treatment defines fair shares relative to participants' own valuations and introduces two-person Divider-Chooser procedures before more complex fair division.

misconceptions: Assumes that equal physical amounts are necessarily fair even when participants value them differently.
Judges fairness from total market value alone instead of each participant's own valuation.
Assumes each participant's claim can be handled independently of the other participants' claims.
Treats an allocation as fair because it looks balanced without checking each person's minimum fair share.
Assumes a two-person divide-and-choose procedure automatically resolves any multi-person allocation.
Assumes a fair allocation must give every participant the same items or the same numerical value.

misconception_provenance.source: Curator-authored after reviewing the expert exercise's task description and design analysis; these may overlap with expert-anticipated pathways.
misconception_provenance.limitation: Not Eedi labels, not student-validated, and not evidence of observed learner behavior.

pilot_protocol.sampling: One scheduled attempt in each of V1, V2, V3, and PIPELINE; preserve every blocked or failed attempt.
pilot_protocol.holdout_rule: The exact reference problem statement, names, numbers, and solution are withheld from generation inputs. V2 hypotheses were written after consulting expert design descriptions and may expose overlapping conceptual contrasts; V2 is not a blind held-out condition.
pilot_protocol.v2_treatment: Six curator-authored hypotheses informed by the expert design analysis; exploratory only, not student-validated, and not equivalent to the historically Eedi-labeled V2 condition.
pilot_protocol.interpretation: One attempt per condition is descriptive calibration only; automated ratings are model judgments, not human/student evidence.

protocol.comparison_scope: Twelve-attempt exploratory pilot across three expert-task directions; one attempt per condition and direction.
protocol.rating_policy: Use the runner's frozen rubric rating only as a model judgment; inspect task outputs and blocked cases separately.
protocol.failure_policy: Do not replace blocked, malformed, interrupted, or failed attempts.
protocol.mathematics_policy: PIPELINE arithmetic/checker outcomes are distinct from PF quality; unsupported or blocked checks are not scored as task defects without case-level evidence.
protocol.limitation: The V2 hypothesis source differs from the historical Eedi treatment; n=1 per direction-condition does not support causal or statistical claims. The current PIPELINE checker may not represent a full fair-division allocation.
